c.tagline: Where a laid-back river capital hides colonial charm in tropical heat.

taxi.fareNote: Meters exist and should be used, but flat fares are common from the airport or bus terminal; confirm the price before departing.

emergency.note: 911 is Paraguay's unified national emergency number covering police, fire, and ambulance dispatch.

hood_landmark.Recoleta: Jardín Botánico y Zoológico de Asunción

avoid.reason: Caution around Mercado 4 and the centre at night

hood_desc: The colonial-era heart of the city along the bay, with government buildings, Plaza de los Héroes, budget hostels and historic hotels; suits history-focused travelers and budget backpackers.
An upscale residential and commercial district built around Shopping del Sol, with modern towers, restaurants and business hotels; suits business travelers and those wanting shopping/dining nearby.
A leafy, quiet embassy district near the Botanical Garden and Zoo, popular for its calm streets and boutique lodging; suits travelers wanting a residential, low-key base.
A modern business corridor near the World Trade Center with corporate hotels and shopping; suits corporate travelers and conference visitors.
The redeveloped waterfront park along the Bahía de Asunción, walkable and scenic with nearby hostels and hotels; suits travelers who want river views and an easy walk into downtown.
lodging: Moderno Dpto con Vista a la Bahía de Asunción

water.note: Stick to bottled or filtered water; tap water quality is inconsistent.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash to the driver or conductor on most routes, though electronic fare cards became mandatory on many lines starting in 2020. Exact change is helpful since buses rarely carry large amounts of change.
transit.hours: Buses generally run from about 5:00 to 23:00 with no unified schedule or map; there is no dedicated night bus network, so taxis or ride apps are used late at night.
transit.note: Routes are numbered but variations (e.g. 30, 30.1, 30.2) serve different sub-routes, so confirm with the driver before boarding.

bus: Terminal de Ómnibus de Asunción (domestic and international coaches)
ferry: Chaco'í passenger/vehicle ferry across the Paraguay River

tip.r: Tipping is not obligatory; rounding up or leaving about 10% in restaurants is appreciated but not expected elsewhere.

food.name: Chipa
food.desc: Ring-shaped bread of cassava starch, cheese, egg and aniseed, eaten warm; sold from baskets on buses, street corners and every bus terminal.

places.name: Na Eustaquia
places.note: Homegrown chain built on Paraguayan snacks; chipa, mbeju and empanadas made through the day.

places.name: Mercado 4 chipa vendors
places.note: Basket sellers work the market aisles from early morning; buy it while it is still hot.

places.name: Lido Bar
places.note: Counter-only institution opposite the Panteon serving chipa and chipa guasu since 1953.

food.name: Sopa paraguaya
food.desc: Famously not a soup: a dense savoury cornbread baked with cornmeal, fresh cheese, onion, milk and eggs, cut in squares beside grilled meat.

places.name: Lido Bar
places.note: Old-school horseshoe counter where sopa paraguaya comes with vori vori and pira caldo.

places.name: Restaurante Bolsi
places.note: Long-running downtown restaurant praised for its typical Paraguayan plates and desserts.

places.name: Na Eustaquia
places.note: Reliable everyday version alongside chipa and bife koygua.

food.name: Mbeju
food.desc: Guarani cassava-starch flatbread bound with cheese and fat, cooked in a dry pan until it holds together; chewy, salty and eaten by hand.

places.name: Na Eustaquia
places.note: Makes mbeju to order through the day; the easiest place to try it properly hot.

places.name: Mercado 4 food stalls
places.note: Griddles at the market turn out mbeju and chipa so'o for a few thousand guaranies.

places.name: Bar San Roque
places.note: Claims to be the oldest restaurant in Asuncion, with the traditional starches on the menu.

food.name: Asado
food.desc: Paraguayan beef grilled slowly over wood or charcoal and salted simply, served with mandioca, sopa paraguaya and chimichurri; the weekend ritual.

places.name: Paulista Grill
places.note: Churrascaria-style grill, a long-standing Asuncion address for endless cuts of beef.

places.name: Talleyrand
places.note: Formal old-guard restaurant that has been grilling Paraguayan beef for decades.

places.name: Restaurante Bolsi
places.note: Open until the small hours with good meat cuts and the city's best-known empanadas.

food.name: Vori vori
food.desc: Thick chicken broth with little balls of cornmeal and cheese dropped in and simmered until they swell; Paraguay's cold-weather comfort soup.

places.name: Lido Bar
places.note: The classic bowl of vori vori, eaten elbow to elbow at the counter.

places.name: Bar San Roque
places.note: Century-old bar serving the traditional soups in a tiled, unchanged dining room.

places.name: Restaurante Bolsi
places.note: Dependable vori vori and pira caldo on a menu that runs late into the night.

food.name: Chipa guasu
food.desc: A moist baked pudding of fresh corn, cheese, milk and onion, softer and sweeter than sopa paraguaya; the standard side at any asado.

places.name: Lido Bar
places.note: Regulars order chipa guasu with mandi'o chyryry as a full downtown lunch.

places.name: Restaurante Bolsi
places.note: Reviewers single out the sopa paraguaya and chipa guasu here.

places.name: Tierra Colorada Gastro
places.note: Chef Rodolfo Angenscheidt reworks Guarani corn and cassava dishes with French technique.

food.name: Terere
food.desc: Yerba mate drunk ice cold from a guampa through a bombilla, the water infused with pounded medicinal herbs; Paraguay's national daily ritual.

places.name: Costanera de Asuncion
places.note: Riverside promenade where whole families sit with thermos and guampa at sunset.

places.name: Plaza Uruguaya yuyo stands
places.note: Yuyeras pound fresh herbs to order for your terere water; ask for menta and cedron.

places.name: Mercado 4 yuyeras
places.note: The biggest concentration of herb sellers in the city, with advice on what each yuyo does.

food.name: Mosto de cana
food.desc: Sugarcane pressed on the spot into a cloudy green juice served over ice with lemon; sold by street carts and market stalls all summer.

places.name: Mercado 4 juice stalls
places.note: Cane presses grind all morning; the cheapest cold drink in the city.

places.name: Lido Bar
places.note: Serves mosto and fresh fruit juices with the traditional plates at the counter.

places.name: Na Eustaquia
places.note: Pairs mosto with chipa and mbeju for a full Paraguayan merienda.

landmarks: Palacio de los López
This gleaming white presidential palace overlooking the Paraguay River is Asunción's most photographed government building, especially striking when illuminated at night.
Panteón Nacional de los Héroes
Modeled after Les Invalides in Paris, this domed mausoleum honors Paraguay's war heroes and stands as a solemn, dignified symbol in the city's historic center.
Asunción Metropolitan Cathedral
This neoclassical cathedral on the Plaza de la Independencia showcases ornate colonial-era religious art and remains the spiritual heart of Paraguay's capital.
Manzana de la Rivera
A cluster of restored 19th-century houses forming a cultural complex and museum, offering a charming glimpse into Asunción's architectural and social history.
Costanera de Asunción
This modern riverfront promenade along the Paraguay River is popular for sunset views, cycling, and leisurely strolls with the city skyline as a backdrop.
Casa de la Independencia
The modest colonial house where Paraguay's independence movement was plotted in 1811 now serves as a museum preserving the nation's founding history.
Estadio Defensores del Chaco
Paraguay's largest football stadium is a passionate gathering point for fans and hosts the national team's biggest matches, embodying the country's football fervor.
Antigua Estación Central del Ferrocarril
This beautifully preserved 19th-century railway station, one of South America's oldest, now operates as a museum celebrating Paraguay's pioneering rail history.
Congreso Nacional
Paraguay's modern National Congress building rises prominently along the riverfront, representing the country's legislative power with striking contemporary architecture.
Jardín Botánico y Zoológico de Asunción
This expansive green retreat combines botanical gardens, a zoo, and historic buildings, providing a peaceful escape from the city and a home to native wildlife.

train.note: Paraguay has no regular passenger rail service. Only an occasional heritage steam tourist train runs at Sapucai, and an Asuncion–Ypacarai suburban revival remains a long-delayed project. Travel overland by bus instead.

bus.note: International coaches depart the Terminal de Ómnibus de Asunción (EBA). Expreso Paraguay and others also run to São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro in high season. Carry your passport; buses stop for immigration at the border.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferries. Asuncion sits on the Paraguay River but river passenger service is minimal; small launches cross to Chaco'i on the far bank.
